questions.question: Under USP <1116>, to which environments do the guidance and microbiological monitoring parameters of this chapter apply?

options.A: All ISO-classified environments, including equipment and component preparation areas and non-sterile product manufacturing areas
options.B: Only cleanrooms, RABS, and isolators used for aseptic processing
options.C: Only conventional cleanrooms; isolators and RABS are covered by other requirements
options.D: Only the ISO 5 critical zone within aseptic processing; other classified areas are not covered

questions.explanation: <1116> states explicitly that the guidance and monitoring parameters apply only to cleanrooms, RABS, and isolators used for aseptic processing; ISO-classified environments used for other purposes need not meet the level of contamination control required for sterile products. The option "All ISO-classified environments" extends the scope to non-sterile uses, contrary to the text.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Introduction (paragraph 2)

questions.question: How does <1116> distinguish the terms sterile and aseptic?

options.A: They are synonyms, both meaning that no viable microorganisms are present in the product and environment at the end of the process
options.B: Sterile means handling sterilized materials in a controlled environment; aseptic means the complete absence of any viable microorganisms
options.C: Sterile means the complete absence of viable microorganisms; aseptic means handling sterilized materials in a controlled environment
options.D: Sterile refers only to terminally sterilized products; aseptic refers only to products sterilized by filtration without terminal sterilization, so they apply to different objects

questions.explanation: The text states that aseptic and sterile are not synonyms: sterile means the complete absence of viable microorganisms, whereas aseptic means handling sterilized materials in a controlled environment so that contamination is kept to a level of known, very low risk. The options that reverse the two definitions are wrong.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Introduction (paragraph 3); Glossary: Aseptic, Sterility

questions.question: Several consecutive environmental monitoring results in an ISO 5 filling zone show zero recovery, and a manager says, "This proves the environment is sterile." Per <1116>, what is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Agree; zero recovery means the environment has reached a sterile state, and gowning and intervention controls can be relaxed accordingly
options.B: Agree, but only for isolators; in conventional cleanrooms zero recovery still cannot be taken as evidence of a sterile environment
options.C: Disagree; zero recovery is due to an overly sensitive sampler, and a less sensitive sampler should be used to match reality
options.D: Disagree; zero recovery only means the count is below the detection limit of the analytical system, and EM can only show that the system is in a consistent state of control

questions.explanation: <1116> states that no method can demonstrate that an aseptic processing environment is sterile; EM results can neither prove nor disprove sterility, and zero only means below the limit of detection. The value of EM is in confirming that the production system is in a consistent, validated state of control.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Introduction; Further Considerations About Data Interpretation

questions.question: Some manufacturers operate RABS in a way that allows open, direct human intervention. Why does <1116> consider such a RABS not to be advanced aseptic processing?

options.A: Operated open, it resembles a conventional cleanroom and no longer effectively separates the operator
options.B: The RABS design cannot achieve ISO 5 particle levels, so it cannot be an advanced technology
options.C: RABS must always use sterilized coveralls, which cannot be satisfied during open operation
options.D: RABS airflow is turbulent, and once opened the unidirectional airflow pattern fails completely

questions.explanation: The premise of advanced aseptic technology is that processing does not rely on direct operator intervention. A RABS operated open, with direct human intervention, behaves more like a conventional cleanroom, so it cannot be counted as an advanced technology; only closed RABS that are never opened, isolators, and the like qualify.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Clean Room Classification for Aseptic Processing Environments (open vs closed RABS); Advanced Aseptic Technologies

questions.question: Under what condition does the argument "the lower the total particle count in a cleanroom, the less likely microorganisms are present in the air" hold?

options.A: Only in areas with HEPA filtration and more than 100 air changes per hour
options.B: Only when the main source of particles is personnel, because particles generated by equipment are almost all non-viable
options.C: Only when the particle counter can detect particles smaller than 0.5 µm
options.D: In all cleanrooms, so EM can monitor only particles and omit microbial monitoring

questions.explanation: People are the only significant source of microbial contamination, but non-viable particles can also come from equipment, and these almost never carry viable organisms. The argument therefore holds only when personnel are the main source of particles, which is why an EM program needs both particle and microbial components.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Clean Room Classification for Aseptic Processing Environments

questions.question: Which statement about settling plates is consistent with <1116>?

options.A: They give only quantitative assessment, and a 30-minute exposure can completely replace active air sampling in the critical zone
options.B: They are suitable only for ISO 8 background areas, should not be placed near the critical zone so as not to disturb unidirectional airflow, and may not be used for any qualitative assessment or trending
options.C: An exposure of 4 to 5 hours provides an adequate limit of detection, and they are especially useful in critical zones where active sampling might interfere with aseptic operations
options.D: Because they require a vacuum pump and power cord, they would disturb unidirectional airflow when used in the critical zone, and therefore may not be used there

questions.explanation: The text states that settling plates are a simple, inexpensive qualitative assessment; an exposure of 4–5 hours provides an adequate limit of detection, and they are especially useful in critical zones where active sampling is intrusive and might compromise aseptic operations. Settling plates do not require a vacuum pump.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Sampling Airborne Microorganisms › Settling Plates

questions.question: When very low airborne microbial levels are expected, <1116> recommends sampling at least 1 cubic meter of air to improve sensitivity. With a slit-to-agar sampler running at 80 L/min, about how long does the text say it takes to sample 1 cubic meter?

options.A: About 15 minutes
options.B: About 2.5 minutes
options.C: About 45 minutes
options.D: About 150 minutes

questions.explanation: The text states that a typical STA sample rate is 80 L/min, so sampling 1 cubic meter requires about 15 minutes of exposure, and longer periods may be needed to obtain representative samples. If the sample volume is too small (for example, only 200 L), sensitivity is insufficient for environments with very low contamination.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Sampling Airborne Microorganisms (1 m³ sample volume, slit-to-agar 80 L/min)

questions.question: For monitoring surfaces that directly contact sterile parts or product, what does <1116> require?

options.A: Sampling should be done during filling so as to reflect actual production risk, and the results may be used for batch release
options.B: Sampling should be done immediately after every personnel intervention, and the batch is rejected if results exceed limits
options.C: As long as contact plates are used, sampling may be done at any time during production without considering residual medium
options.D: It should be done after production operations are complete, and because surface sampling is not a sterility test, it should not be used as a criterion for product release or rejection

questions.explanation: The text requires that surface monitoring of product-contact surfaces be performed only after production operations are complete, and states explicitly that surface sampling is not a sterility test and should not be used as a criterion for release or rejection; because sampling is performed aseptically by personnel, it is difficult to determine whether recovered contamination is related to the product.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Surface Sampling

questions.question: The product-contact parts of a filling machine have many irregular grooves that a contact plate cannot sample effectively. What does <1116> recommend?

options.A: No sampling is needed, because irregular surfaces do not affect the product and periodic visual inspection of the parts is enough
options.B: Use a swab, defining the area with a sterile template (about 24–30 cm²), and report results per swab
options.C: Use a settling plate beside the grooves, exposed for a period, and report results per 4 hours
options.D: Use a gelatin filter sampler to filter the air directly above the groove surface, and report results per cubic meter

questions.explanation: Contact plates are for flat surfaces; swabs supplement them for irregular surfaces (especially equipment surfaces), with a sterile template defining the sampled area, generally about 24–30 cm²; after swabbing, the swab is placed in diluent or transport medium and then incubated, and results are reported per swab for the defined sampled area.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Surface Sampling

questions.question: When laboratory resources are limited and not all isolates can be identified, what order of priority does <1116> recommend?

options.A: Isolates from non-critical areas first, because the flora there best represents the overall condition and long-term trends of the whole facility
options.B: Identify only samples with more than 15 cfu; samples below this value never need identification
options.C: Isolates from the critical zone and immediately adjacent areas first, with identification methods verified and kits validated for their intended use
options.D: Identify in order of sampling date, without considering the grade of the sampled area or the source of the isolate

questions.explanation: The text requires that isolates from the critical zone and its immediately adjacent areas be identified in preference to those from non-critical areas; identification methods should be verified, and commercial kits should also be validated for their intended use. Flora information can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of cleaning and disinfection and, when the incidence limit is exceeded, to help trace the source of contamination.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Identification of Microbial Isolates

questions.question: Why does <1116> say the difference between an alert level of 1 cfu and an action level of 3 cfu is not analytically significant?

options.A: Microbial recovery has a normal variability of about ±0.5 log10, and variability between commonly used active samplers can be as much as tenfold
options.B: Because cfu counts in ISO 5 should never exceed 1, so a limit of 3 cfu is meaningless
options.C: Because alert and action levels should be set arbitrarily by managers based on experience, with no data needed
options.D: Because EU GMP and USP contradict each other on cfu limits, and one must be chosen

questions.explanation: The normal variability of microbial growth and recovery tests is about ±0.5 log10, and samplers can differ by as much as tenfold, so values within a five- to ten-fold range may not be significantly different. Treating differences within the normal variability range as different values is therefore not scientifically valid and may trigger unnecessary action.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Microbiological Control Parameters in Clean Rooms, Isolators, and RABS

questions.question: According to <1116> Table 3, what is the recommended initial contamination recovery rate for active air sampling in an ISO 7 environment?
questions.explanation: The initial recovery rates recommended in Table 3 are: isolators/closed RABS <0.1%, ISO 5 <1%, ISO 6 <3%, ISO 7 <5%, ISO 8 <10%. These are incidence rates expressed as percentages, not cfu limits.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Microbiological Control Parameters in Clean Rooms, Isolators, and RABS, Table 3

questions.question: In an ISO 5 area, 200 active air samples were taken in one month, and 3 showed colonies (1, 2, and 1 cfu). Under <1116>, what is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: The recovery rate is 1.5%, which meets the ISO 5 recommendation because each sample's cfu count is very low, so no action is needed
options.B: The recovery rate is 1.5%, exceeding the ISO 5 recommendation of <1%, so corrective action such as reviewing disinfection, personnel, and sampling should be taken
options.C: The recovery rate is 3%, between the ISO 5 and ISO 7 recommendations, so maintain the status quo and keep watching the trend
options.D: The recovery rate is 0.015%, far below all recommended values, so no action or trend follow-up is needed

questions.explanation: The recovery rate is the number of samples with growth divided by the total number of samples: 3/200 = 1.5%, which exceeds the ISO 5 recommendation of <1%, and Table 3 calls for corrective action when the incidence is exceeded. What matters is the proportion of samples with growth, not the cfu count of each sample.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Microbiological Control Parameters in Clean Rooms, Isolators, and RABS, Table 3

questions.question: A single active air sample in an ISO 5 area recovers 18 cfu. Per <1116>, which action is most appropriate?

options.A: Treat it as normal fluctuation because it does not reach the 25 cfu limit, with no investigation or trend review
options.B: Resample a few days later, and if the resample is normal, close the matter without reviewing earlier data
options.C: Launch a thorough investigation, reviewing recovery rates and identification results for at least two weeks before the event to find relevant patterns
options.D: Declare the batch rejected outright, because a single sample has exceeded 15 cfu, with no further evaluation

questions.explanation: A single ISO 5 sample exceeding about 15 cfu should trigger a careful and thorough investigation, including review of recovery rates for at least two weeks before the event. Resampling a few days later has little value because the conditions cannot be reproduced exactly, and EM results cannot by themselves be the basis for rejecting a batch.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Significant Excursions

questions.question: Which approach does <1116> regard as the best way to achieve sterility assurance?

options.A: Focusing on contamination brought by personnel and on facility design that reduces this risk, such as reducing human intervention and providing sufficient air changes
options.B: Increasing sampling frequency and the number of sampling sites so that EM data are representative of every batch
options.C: Using zero EM results as the basis for batch release in place of the sterility test
options.D: Raising the alert and action level values to reduce the number of investigations

questions.explanation: The text states that sterility assurance is best achieved by focusing on contamination brought by personnel and on facility designs that reduce this risk; the greatest risk reduction comes from using equipment design to reduce or eliminate human intervention and providing sufficient air changes for the number of personnel. EM can only confirm that the system is in a consistent state of control.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Further Considerations About Data Interpretation

questions.question: An operator with cold symptoms is scheduled to work on an isolator filling line. Per <1116>, how should this be handled?

options.A: They may enter, because the isolator completely separates the operator from the critical zone, so health status need not be considered
options.B: They may enter, provided they add a second pair of gloves and additionally disinfect their hands before entering
options.C: They may enter, provided they do not enter the ISO 5 area or touch product-contact surfaces, wear a mask and double gloves throughout, and notify the supervisor beforehand
options.D: They may not; ill personnel must not enter even where an isolator, blow/fill/seal, or closed RABS is used

questions.explanation: The text explicitly requires that only healthy personnel enter controlled environments; ill personnel must not enter even aseptic environments using advanced technologies such as isolators, blow/fill/seal, or closed RABS. People are the only significant source of contamination in aseptic environments.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Training of Personnel

questions.question: To reduce the risk of leakage at the glove-sleeve junction, which practice does <1116> suggest considering?

options.A: Use shorter sleeves that expose the wrist to make glove changes easier, and add a sleeve cover over the gloves
options.B: Cover the skin as completely as possible, and consider using sleeve covers or tape to seal the glove-sleeve junction
options.C: Replace sterile garments with ordinary cleanroom garments to reduce friction and particle generation between garments and gloves
options.D: Allow a little exposed skin in conventional cleanrooms, as long as that area is not within the ISO 5 zone

questions.explanation: Aseptic operations should use sterilized garments with the best filtration performance and cover the skin as completely as possible, considering sleeve covers or tape to reduce leakage at the critical glove-sleeve junction; exposed skin should never be visible in a conventional cleanroom under any circumstances.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Training of Personnel

questions.question: Why does <1116> require that personnel who take environmental monitoring samples also receive formal, documented training?

options.A: In highly automated operations, sampling personnel may be the people who most often come into direct contact with critical surfaces and areas, and improper technique can itself cause contamination
options.B: Because sampling personnel must be able to decide alert/action levels themselves and determine whether batches can be released
options.C: Because the training records of sampling personnel can replace confirmation of gowning qualification for production operators
options.D: Because the main source of microbial contamination is the sampling equipment, not people

questions.explanation: The text notes that in highly automated operations, monitoring personnel may be the employees with the most direct contact with critical surfaces in the process area, and improper sampling technique or entry near the critical zone may cause contamination; all personnel entering controlled environments therefore need documented formal training, and aseptic technique during interventions should be as close to perfect as possible.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Training of Personnel

questions.question: Routine EM on an isolator filling line finds microbial contamination near a glove port. Per <1116>, which are the most likely causes in this type of system?

options.A: Small changes in ambient temperature and relative humidity causing microbial proliferation and spread near the glove port
options.B: Lot-to-lot differences in sampling media causing inadequate growth promotion and biased recovery results
options.C: Loss of glove integrity, or inadvertent introduction of materials that have not been decontaminated into the system
options.D: An operator in the gowning room outside the system using a different brand of disinfectant than usual, causing residues

questions.explanation: The text states that in closed RABS and isolators, loss of glove integrity or accidental introduction of materials that have not been decontaminated are among the most likely causes when microbial contamination is detected. An investigation also reviews maintenance and disinfection records, non-routine events, temperature and humidity, and personnel training status.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Importance of a Microbiological Evaluation Program for Controlled Environments (investigation of increased recovery rates)

questions.question: After the recovery rate rises, the floor wants to increase the number of samples taken during production immediately. What is <1116>'s view?

options.A: It must be increased; this is the highest-priority corrective action with no risk, and should be carried out in production immediately
options.B: No corrective action is needed, because contamination events usually disappear by themselves and more sampling only wastes resources
options.C: All sampling should stop until the investigation reaches a clear conclusion, to avoid further disturbing the aseptic environment
options.D: It is not necessarily appropriate while aseptic operations are in progress, because intrusive or excessively dense sampling can increase contamination risk

questions.explanation: Increasing sampling frequency is one possible corrective action, but the text cautions that during aseptic operations, intrusive or excessively dense sampling can increase contamination risk. Other feasible corrective actions include strengthening personnel training, increasing disinfection or changing disinfectants, and identifying the contaminants and tracing their source.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Importance of a Microbiological Evaluation Program for Controlled Environments (corrective actions); USP <1116> Microbiological Control Parameters in Clean Rooms, Isolators, and RABS (Table 3 corrective actions)

questions.question: According to <1116> Table 2, what is the recommended frequency of active air sampling in the critical zone (ISO 5 or better) of an isolator?

options.A: Once per operating shift, the same as the critical zone of a conventional cleanroom
options.B: Once per week
options.C: Once per day
options.D: Once per month

questions.explanation: In Table 2, active air sampling of the critical zone is each operating shift for cleanrooms/RABS and once per day for isolators; all sampling of the non-sterile area surrounding an isolator is once per month. The difference in frequency reflects the reduced risk of personnel contamination with an isolator.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Establishment of Sampling Plan and Sites, Table 2

questions.question: Which statement about the critical zone in aseptic processing is consistent with <1116>?

options.A: The area where containers, stoppers, and product are exposed is always ISO 5 and should be treated as a sterile field; non-sterile objects, including gloved hands, must not touch it
options.B: Depending on process risk and monitoring results, the exposed area may be downgraded to ISO 6, as long as particles continue to be monitored, results meet alert levels, and deviations are documented
options.C: Only the direct product-contact surfaces are the critical zone; the surrounding air and airflow are outside its scope, so the surrounding air need not be classified or controlled
options.D: A hand wearing a sterile glove may touch the filling station, as long as the glove was disinfected before the operation

questions.explanation: The text defines the critical zone as the area where containers, stoppers, and product are exposed to the environment; it is always ISO 5, and the whole area should be treated as a sterile field. Non-sterile objects, including the gloved hands of cleanroom personnel or RABS/isolator gloves, must not touch sterile product, container stoppers, the filling station, or conveying equipment before or during aseptic operations.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Establishment of Sampling Plan and Sites (critical zone)

questions.question: Why does <1116> consider that walls and floors may be sampled relatively infrequently?

options.A: Because no microorganisms grow on walls and floors, so sampling results are always zero
options.B: Because regulations prohibit sampling walls and floors so as not to damage the surfaces
options.C: Because contamination at these locations can only be assessed by particle counters, and microbial sampling does not apply
options.D: Because contamination at these locations is unlikely to affect the product and operators should not touch walls or floors, although sampling can still reflect the effectiveness of the disinfection program

questions.explanation: The text states that wall and floor sampling can provide information on the effectiveness of the disinfection program, but because contamination there is unlikely to affect the product and operators should not touch them, sampling can be relatively infrequent. Sampling sites should be selected first on the basis of personnel activity, and the most important are air contamination near exposed sterile materials, entry points where materials pass from lower to higher grades, and the vicinity of doors and airlocks.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Selection of Sample Sites within Clean Rooms and Aseptic Processing Areas

questions.question: What typical conditions does <1116> describe for incubating general media (such as SCDM) for environmental monitoring?

options.A: Fixed at 55°C for 24 hours, with no need to adjust temperature and time to the type of microorganism
options.B: A range of about 20°–35°, incubated for not less than 72 hours; longer may be considered for contaminants known to grow slowly
options.C: Only at 2°–8° for 7 days, and any high-temperature incubation is prohibited so as not to kill environmental microorganisms
options.D: Only at 35° for 24 hours; results from incubation beyond 24 hours should not be used, to avoid over-counting

questions.explanation: The text states that the incubation temperature for general media such as SCDM is usually in the range of about 20°–35°, with an incubation time of not less than 72 hours. Absent confirmatory evidence, a single plate may be incubated at a lower temperature followed by a higher temperature, but incubating first at the lower temperature may affect the recovery of personnel-associated Gram-positive cocci.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Critical Factors in the Design and Implementation of a Microbiological Environmental Monitoring Program › Selection of Culture Conditions

questions.question: Two rooms are both ISO 7: one is an aseptic process support area and the other is a lower-risk operating area. What is <1116>'s view on their sampling frequency and level of control?

options.A: With the same classification, they should use exactly the same sampling frequency and level of control to maintain consistency and comparability
options.B: Sampling should be increased by a fixed multiple according to each room's classification, and the more samples the better, without considering risk
options.C: They need not be the same; they should be determined by prospective risk analysis and process activities, and both oversampling and undersampling damage control
options.D: Only particle classification needs to be considered; microbial sampling frequency is directly specified by ISO 14644, with no separate risk assessment needed

questions.explanation: The text states that cleanroom classification helps establish levels of control, but it does not mean that rooms of the same grade should all have the same level of control and monitoring frequency; users should perform a prospective risk analysis to justify the sampling locations and frequencies for each controlled environment. Oversampling can be as harmful as undersampling.
questions.reference: USP <1116> Establishment of Sampling Plan and Sites (prospective risk analysis)
